passages.happening:
‘And David sang this song to the LORD on the day the LORD had delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul’ (verse 1).

He begins with a burst of names for God: “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer. My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation. My stronghold, my refuge, and my Savior, You save me from violence” (verses 2-3).

Then he tells what happened. ‘For the waves of death engulfed me; the torrents of chaos overwhelmed me. The cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me’ (verses 5-6). “In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God. And from His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for help reached His ears” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
After all the violence, betrayal and grief of the chapters before, the book pauses to let David speak to God, and what he says is praise. The song sits at the center of the closing collection, paired with his last words in chapter 23. Its heading places it on the day of his rescue from all his enemies and from Saul, a summary of his whole life from fugitive to king.

The same song, with many small differences, is Psalm 18. Most scholars think it an old royal hymn. Its Hebrew has archaic forms, and many specialists count it among the older poems in the Bible. The two versions show how sacred songs were kept and sung in slightly different forms, with no one thinking either false.

The names for God come from a soldier's life. Rock, fortress, stronghold and shield are the language of a man who hid among the crags of the wilderness of Judah and fought in the field. The horn is the horn of a wild ox, a picture of strength. Rock, in Hebrew tsur, a massive cliff or boulder, names God four times in the song: in a land of wilderness crags, a rock meant shelter that does not move.

The waves of death and the cords of Sheol picture death as deep water and a hunter's snare. Sheol is the Old Testament's name for the realm of the dead, the grave and the shadowy place beyond it.
passages.later: The song is kept a second time in the Psalms, with a line of its own at the start: ‘I love You, O LORD, my strength’ (Psalm 18:1).
passages.asks: David piles up names for God: rock, fortress, shield, refuge. Ask which of them speaks to the place you are in now. And ask whether you have ever told God, in words of your own, what he has brought you through.

passages.t: God comes down in the storm
passages.happening:
Then the earth shakes. God comes down in fury, with smoke and consuming fire. ‘He parted the heavens and came down with dark clouds beneath His feet’ (verse 10). He rides a cherub and soars on the wings of the wind. He makes darkness his canopy. The LORD thunders from heaven, shoots his arrows and hurls lightning, and the channels of the sea are laid bare (verses 8-16).

“He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters. He rescued me from my powerful enemy, from foes too mighty for me” (verses 17-18). ‘He brought me out into the open; He rescued me because He delighted in me’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
This is Hebrew poetry, built on pairs of lines in which the second echoes, sharpens or extends the first. Here the song tells David's rescue as a storm in which God himself appears.

The pictures come from the world around Israel. Neighboring peoples spoke of their storm god, Baal in Canaan, as the rider of the clouds. Israel's poets used that shared language to say that it is the LORD, not Baal, who commands the storm and the sea. The cherub God rides is one of the winged guardian creatures pictured above the ark and in the temple.

The song does not describe the weather of one battle. It shows what the rescue looked like from heaven's side: God moved earth and sky to reach one man who cried out to him. And the reason it gives is simple. God rescued him because he delighted in him.
passages.later: The storm recalls the day God came down on Sinai, when ‘there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud was upon the mountain’ (Exodus 19:16).
passages.asks: The song pictures heaven and earth shaken to rescue one person. Ask what it means to you that God hears a single cry for help. And ask what deep waters you would name if you prayed this part of the song today.

passages.happening:
Then David says why God rescued him. “The LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness; He has repaid me according to the cleanness of my hands” (verse 21). He has kept the LORD's ways and not turned from his God. ‘And I have been blameless before Him and kept myself from iniquity’ (verse 24).

Then he turns to God's ways with people: ‘To the faithful You show Yourself faithful, to the blameless You show Yourself blameless; to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd’ (verses 26-27). ‘You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The middle of the song reflects on why God rescued David: the LORD rewards faithfulness. Verses 26 and 27 are a neat set of mirror lines. God meets each person in kind, faithful to the faithful, and shrewd to the crooked. The crooked person finds God turning every twist back on him.

Clean hands meant hands that had not done violence or taken bribes. The heading ties the song to David's rescue from Saul, the years when he twice could have killed the king and would not.

The word for blameless means whole, with integrity. It is a claim that sits hard beside the Bathsheba story, and readers have to hold both together.
passages.later: The same book that keeps this song tells of David's sin with Bathsheba, and the heading of Psalm 51 sets that psalm ‘When Nathan the prophet came to him after his adultery with Bathsheba’ (Psalm 51:1). The Bible does not ask a reader to forget one when reading the other.
passages.hard:
How can David claim to be righteous and blameless after his sin with Bathsheba and Uriah?

The difficulty is real, especially since the song comes after that story in the book. Several answers are given. Many interpreters note that the heading ties the song to his rescue from Saul, an earlier time when David had refused to harm the LORD's anointed and acted with integrity. Others point out that blameless in the Old Testament means wholehearted loyalty to God, not sinlessness: David never worshiped another god, and when he was confronted he repented. Still others read the song as a royal hymn describing what the king was called to be, with the book's honest record of David's failures as its counterweight.

The Bible does not ask readers to forget chapter 11 when they read chapter 22.
passages.asks: David could speak of clean hands about one part of his life and not another. Ask where your own life has integrity, and where it does not. And ask whether you can thank God for the first without hiding the second.

passages.t: Strength for battle, and praise among the nations
passages.happening:
“For You, O LORD, are my lamp; the LORD lights up my darkness” (verse 29). With God, David says, he can charge an army and scale a wall. ‘As for God, His way is perfect; the word of the LORD is flawless’ (verse 31). “For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?” (verse 32).

God trains his hands for battle and makes his feet like a deer's on the heights. David pursues his enemies and crushes them, and nations come to serve him (verses 33-46).

“The LORD lives, and blessed be my Rock!” (verse 47). ‘Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name’ (verse 50). The song ends with the promise: “Great salvation He brings to His king. He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever” (verse 51).
passages.hearers:
The last part of the song praises God for victory in battle and rule over nations. Deer move safely on rocky heights where people fall, and the king is given that sure step. A bow of bronze is a picture of strength beyond ordinary strength.

The battle lines belong to the wars of an ancient king, and the song speaks of them in the plain language of its time. But it puts every victory in God's hands. The title Rock frames the whole song, and it ends not with David but with God's loving devotion to his anointed king and his line. That last line reaches back to the promise of chapter 7.

The word for anointed is mashiach. Kings were anointed with oil as a sign that God had chosen them. Because the promise reached to David's descendants forever, later Israel looked for an anointed king from David's line, and the Greek form of the word is Christos, Christ.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 50, from its twin in the Psalms, to show that God always meant the nations to praise him: “Therefore I will praise You among the Gentiles; I will sing hymns to Your name” (Romans 15:9).
passages.hard:
How should a reader take a king's war song: ‘I ground them as the dust of the earth’ (verse 43)?

First, as history. This is the song of a real king in an age of war, and the Bible does not hide it. Second, the song itself puts every victory in God's hands, and it ends in praise among the nations, not over them; Paul takes that line as the nations joining the praise. Third, no reading of this song gives any modern nation or army the place of God's anointed king, and none makes it right to hate an enemy.
passages.asks: The song ends with God's love for his anointed, not with David's victories. Ask whose strength you credit when things go well. And ask what it would look like for your own praise to make room for people who are not like you.
